hints.content:
Let's separate the variables.

$\begin{align}
\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=f(x)g(y)
\\\\
\dfrac{1}{g(y)}\,dy&=f(x)\,dx
\\\\
e^y\,dy&=\dfrac{4}{x}\,dx
\\\\
\displaystyle \int e^y\,dy&=\displaystyle \int \dfrac{4}{x}\,dx
\end{align}$

Ty separated the variables correctly.

Now we isolate $y$.

$\begin{align}
e^y&=4\ln|x|+C
\\\\
\ln(e^y)&=\ln(4\ln|x|+C)
\\\\
y&=\ln(4\ln|x|+C)\end{align}$

Ty has correctly isolated $y$.
In conclusion, Ty's work is correct.

question.content:
Ty tried to solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{4}{xe^{y}}$. This is his work:

$\begin{align}
&&\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{4}{xe^{y}}
\\\\
\text{Step 1:}&&\displaystyle\int e^y\,dy&=\displaystyle\int \dfrac{4}{x}\,dx
\\\\
\text{Step 2:}&&e^y&=4\ln|x|+C
\\\\
\text{Step 3:}&&\ln(e^y)&=\ln(4\ln|x|+C)
\\\\
\text{Step 4:}&&y&=\ln(4\ln|x|+C)
\end{align}$

**Is Ty's work correct? If not, what is his mistake?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

choices.content: **Step 1** is incorrect. The separation of variables was done incorrectly.

choices.clue: When we take the natural logarithm of the left-hand side, we need to take the natural logarithm of the entire right-hand side, including the $C$ term.
choices.content: **Step 3** is incorrect. The right-hand side of the equation should be $\ln(4\ln|x|)+C$.

choices.clue: The equations $y=e^x$ and $y=\ln(x)$ are inverses of each other, so $\ln(e^y)=y$.
choices.content: **Step 4** is incorrect. The left-hand side of the equation should be $|y|$.
